text:
A young monk named Tenzin was struggling with a bitter disappointment. He had spent two years preparing for an important teaching role, but the position was given to someone else. For weeks, he could neither eat nor sleep properly.

He went to his master and poured out his frustration. “I was treated unfairly,” he said. “I keep replaying the moment in my mind, and I feel worse every day.”

The master listened patiently. “When a person is struck by an arrow, he feels pain,” he said. “That is unavoidable. But if a second arrow hits him in exactly the same spot, the pain doubles. Do you know who fires the second arrow?”

Tenzin shook his head.

“He does it himself,” said the master. “The first arrow is the event: the lost position. The second arrow is everything you tell yourself afterwards: ‘I’m not good enough,’ ‘it’s always like this,’ ‘my life is ruined.’ Nobody forces you to fire it.”

Tenzin lowered his eyes. He realised that most of his suffering had come from his own thoughts, not from the decision itself.

“Does this mean I shouldn’t feel anything?” he asked.

“Not at all,” replied the master. “Feel the first arrow honestly. Grieve if you must. But once the pain has been acknowledged, put your bow down.”

That evening, Tenzin sat in the garden and, for the first time in weeks, simply let the sadness exist without arguing with it. By morning, it had lost much of its sting.

Moral: We cannot avoid every misfortune, but we can refuse to multiply it with our own thoughts.

quiz.q: Tenzin did not get the teaching role.
The master said Tenzin should feel nothing.
Feel the first arrow honestly. But once the pain has been acknowledged, put your ___ down.
